extracted.intended_audience: writers and educated readers interested in crafting lyrical essays on manners, gifts, and nature
extracted.subtask_description: Essayistic guidance and norms for composing reflective, lyrical prose about human manners, gifts, and the natural world; useful to creative writers aiming for moral depth and vivid depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuineness of high behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: High behavior must be native and genuine: 'There must be romance of character... It must be genius which takes that direction: it must be not courteous, but courtesy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer manners that spring from character rather than learned etiquette. Anti-patterns: mere polished or studied courtesy that lacks inner generosity. Example positive model: spontaneous, commanding deportment that protects and exhilarates (compared to costume politeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue should be warm with life, not costume
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue ought not to 'strut and bridle' in costume; it should be 'warm with life' rather than merely epigramatic or fashionably witty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid period-costume affectation and artificially epigrammatic speech (criticized in Scott); aim for natural speech that reveals character (Shakspeare praised as exemplary). If dialogue reads as 'in costume' it will not withstand rereading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of manners and character expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners should be original and emanate freely from character rather than be learned conventions: 'whose character emanates freely in their word and gesture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose behavior feels spontaneous and sovereign; a beautiful form or courtly polish that is merely imitated is inferior to an original, commanding manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize beautiful behavior over outward form
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A beautiful form is better than a beautiful face; a beautiful behavior is better than a beautiful form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In valuation and in depiction, internal deportment and moral bearing matter more than physical beauty or ornamental trappings. In fiction and life emphasize conduct and moral presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape fashion's narrow locality to regain perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid being enslaved by fashion and local caprice, change setting: 'To remove your residence a couple of miles, or at most four, will commonly relieve the most extreme susceptibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If social fashions constrict you (or a character), depict or enact geographical or social distance to regain individuality and wider values; fashion's advantages are often local and fade outside their precincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: The only true gift is a portion of thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The only gift is a portion of thyself. Thou must bleed for me. Therefore the poet brings his poem; the shepherd, his lamb; the farmer, corn... the girl, a handkerchief of her own sewing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gifts should be personal, expressive of the giver's life and talent. Anti-patterns: purchased trinkets or jewels that are merely apologies for giving (suitable only for symbolic/state contexts). Good gifts restore social bonds by conveying personal biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowers and fruits are fitting presents
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowers and fruits are 'always fit presents': flowers assert a ray of beauty that outvalues mere utility; fruits are the 'flower of commodities' and can justify the labor of giving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ephemeral, beautiful gifts to express sentiment; they connote effort and proportion between labor and reward (example: traveling a long way to present summer fruit).

rubrics_metrics.name: For common gifts, meet necessity first
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving common gifts, necessity determines pertinence: if someone lacks shoes, provide shoes rather than a paint-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical needs justify and simplify gift choice. In situations of clear need, a necessary gift is both fitting and appreciated; when necessity forces the choice, one need not overthink.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving well is a moral skill
rubrics_metrics.description: He who can receive a gift well is admirable: 'He is a good man who can receive a gift well.' Both excessive joy and excessive shame at receiving are unbecoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should accept gifts without humiliation or over-display of desire; receiving gracefully maintains equality and preserves the social harmony of giving. Avoid treating the gift as an invasion of independence or reacting with servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect commensurability or gratitude for gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no true commensurability between a man and any gift; expecting gratitude is 'mean' and often punished by insensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Givers should not give with calculative expectation of thanks; generosity is best when unconditional. Be prepared for ingratitude and view giving as an expression rather than a transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frivolity and euphuism when writing about nature
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A dilettantism in nature is barren and unworthy... as soon as men begin to write on nature, they fall into euphuism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the subject of nature with seriousness and reserve. Anti-patterns: ornate, superficial, or foppish treatment that betrays lack of true communion with natural objects. Use genuine curiosity and concrete knowledge rather than rhetorical flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature's beauty often needs human moral equals to be fully effective
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The beauty of nature must always seem unreal and mocking, until the landscape has human figures that are as good as itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting landscape, pair it with human figures of moral or imaginative stature to avoid a sense of nature's aloofness; the contrast between corrupt humanity and pristine nature can feel discordant unless humans in the scene match the landscape's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete sensory particulars to render nature's sanctity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emerson lists specific natural particulars—the fall of snowflakes, blowing sleet, waving rye, reflections in lakes, 'musical steaming odorous south wind,' crackling hemlock—as the 'music and pictures of the most ancient religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, multi-sensory details (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory) to make scenes of nature convincing and spiritually resonant. Avoid abstract generalities in favor of specific images and sounds that ground the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give nature scale and perspective through geological/time depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Geology teaches the 'secularity of nature' and the long periods required for rock, life, and human arrival — 'How far off yet is the trilobite!... farther yet to Plato.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke deep time and gradual processes to place human actions in perspective; use long temporal scales to enrich themes, evoke humility, and avoid narrow, presentist judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize unity beneath variety — simple principles underlie complex forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature 'has but one stuff,--but one stuff with its two ends, to serve up all her dream-like variety.' Motion and rest are primary secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition and thought, seek unifying principles that explain apparent diversity. Show how small causes (motion, rest) and simple materials combine over time to produce complexity; this can lend coherence to descriptive or philosophical passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naive rural idealization; be critical of sentimental camping-out remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay cautions against hearing too much of rural influence as a cure-all: 'We can hear too much of rural influences... a boy who thinks camping will make him grand is mistaken; let us be men instead of woodchucks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't romanticize rural life or assume simple immersion in nature is a wholesale solution to moral or aesthetic problems. Show complexity and avoid reductive nostalgia.
